o: Choose k candies maximizing the minimum pairwise price difference. Sort prices; the min difference in any basket is minimized by adjacent picks, so the problem becomes: pick k sorted values maximizing the minimum gap between consecutive picks. Binary search on the answer d: greedily check whether k candies can be placed with all consecutive gaps ≥ d (take the first candy, then each next candy at least d away). Monotonicity makes binary search valid. Example 1: sorted [1,2,5,8,13,21], d=8 achievable via 5,13,21 → answer 8. Example 3: all equal → 0.
k: Sort first; only adjacent gaps within the chosen set matter.
Binary search on d with a greedy feasibility check (first-fit placement).

a.i: Enumerate all C(n, k) baskets, compute min adjacent gap of each. Exponential — only viable for tiny n.
s: Generate all k-subsets of sorted prices.
For each, compute min consecutive difference.

a.n: Approach 2: Binary Search on Answer + Greedy Check (Optimal)
a.i: Feasibility of gap d is monotone: if k candies fit with gaps ≥ d, they fit for any smaller d. Greedy check: sort, always take the first candy, then take each subsequent candy whose price exceeds last-taken + d.
s: Sort price; binary search d in [0, (max−min)/(k−1)].
check(d): count = 1, prev = price[0]; for each p, if p − prev ≥ d, count++, prev = p; return count ≥ k.
a.t: O(n log n + n log(maxRange)) — sort plus binary search with linear checks

w: This is the classic 'aggressive cows' pattern — binary search the answer with a greedy feasibility check. Pitfalls: the greedy check must take the FIRST valid candy each time (first-fit maximizes remaining room); watch integer overflow in gap computations (prices to 1e9). Edge cases: duplicate prices (answer 0), k = n (answer = min adjacent gap). Follow-up: maximize the sum of gaps instead, or handle weighted candies.
